1.grade_fit_note: Proximity agreement with neither/nor plus a tense shift (L.5.1d) suit grade 5.
1.note: With neither/nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'sisters', so 'were'. 'started' requires past 'drove'. A (was+drives) has both errors but 'was' is a common attraction error, so it is still live.

2.grade_fit_note: its/it's and plural possessive apostrophes are L.4-L.5 skills; easy for grade 7.
2.note: 'three teams' coaches' is a plural possessive; 'its' is the possessive pronoun. Clean item, but below grade 7.

3.grade_fit_note: Kinship words used as names vs. after 'my' is a standard grade 5-6 trap.
3.note: 'Grandpa' is used as a name, so it is capitalized; 'my uncle' takes a possessive, so it stays lowercase.

4.grade_fit_note: Contrasting a quoted fragment with a quoted full sentence is a reasonable grade 7-8 item.
4.note: A fragment worked into the sentence ('with real heart') stays lowercase; a quoted full sentence starts with a capital ('Next').

5.grade_fit_note: Correlative conjunctions are named in L.5.1e.
5.note: The pairs are not only...but also and either...or. B gets both pairs wrong and sounds wrong to any native ear.

6.grade_fit_note: Historical periods vs. century numbers are grade 6-7 material.
6.note: 'Middle Ages' names a historical period and is capitalized; 'sixteenth century' is lowercase in Chicago, AP and MLA.

7.grade_fit_note: Commas before tag questions are named in L.5.2c.
7.note: A tag question takes a comma and a question mark. B (no comma, period) is close to dead. This is the only count-axis item whose key uses both marks.

8.grade_fit_note: Coordinate adjectives (L.7.2a) plus an irregular plural possessive.
8.note: There is no comma between the last adjective and its noun, and the possessive is 'children's'. 'childrens'' is a common real error, so every distractor is live.

9.grade_fit_note: Relative adverbs when/where are L.4.1a; the item tests that, not a grade 7 clause skill.
9.note: 'Which' cannot introduce a clause that already has a complete object or locative ('spent spring break', 'painted pictures'), so 'when' and 'where' are needed. B, with 'which...which', reads as plainly broken.

10.grade_fit_note: Coordinate vs. cumulative adjectives is L.7.2a.
10.note: 'long, exhausting' is coordinate and takes a comma; 'tall pine' is cumulative and takes none. A sound test of the distinction.

11.grade_fit_note: Language-derived subjects vs. general subjects; slightly easy for 6 but common error.
11.note: 'English' is capitalized because it comes from a language name; 'geography' is a general subject and stays lowercase.

12.note: The opening modifier must attach to 'Talia', not to her hands, and 'although' cannot also take 'but'. The key is the uniquely shortest option, a minor length tell.

13.grade_fit_note: Parentheses plus nonrestrictive commas match L.6.2a.
13.note: There is no comma after a parenthetical where none would otherwise go. The nonrestrictive 'which' clause needs paired commas; C and D keep only the closing one.

14.grade_fit_note: The restrictive cue 'Only' makes this a fair, slightly hard grade 6 item.
14.note: 'Only the students who finished' is restrictive, so it takes no commas. The clause about the named Mr. Castillo is nonrestrictive and needs paired commas.

15.grade_fit_note: Proper adjectives from nationalities are an early-elementary skill (L.2-L.4).
15.note: The proper adjectives 'Japanese' and 'Canadian' are capitalized, and the common noun 'garden' is not. 'a Japanese garden' is clearly generic. Well below grade 7.

16.grade_fit_note: Pronoun case and intensive pronouns are L.6.1a-b.
16.note: The object of 'asked' takes objective 'me', and the reflexive is 'themselves'. 'Marisol and I' is a highly attractive hypercorrection.

17.grade_fit_note: Pronoun shifts in person (L.6.1c) and case in an appositive.
17.note: 'students' needs 'they', not a shift to 'you'. The object of 'for' is 'us sixth graders'.

18.grade_fit_note: Region vs. compass direction is standard grade 5-6.
18.note: 'Southwest' names a region and is capitalized; 'drove east' is a direction and is not.

19.grade_fit_note: Perfect tenses and tense consistency are L.5.1b-d.
19.note: Past perfect 'had eaten' plus past progressive 'was reading'. A (ate+is) makes both errors and is near-dead.

20.grade_fit_note: Capitalizing street names vs. common nouns is an L.2.2a skill.
20.note: 'Cedar Avenue' is a proper name; 'small lake' is a common noun. Too easy for grade 5.

21.grade_fit_note: Semicolons between independent clauses vs. a comma after an introductory dependent clause.
21.note: The 'Although' clause is dependent and takes a comma. The two independent clauses are joined by a semicolon; B is a comma splice.

22.note: Formal usage requires 'wish I were' and past perfect 'had practiced' in the counterfactual 'if' clause. 'wish I was' (D) is common informally but is not accepted in formal-usage keys, so I did not list it as defensible.

23.grade_fit_note: Commas in a series are L.5.2a; the comma before the verb is the added trap.
23.note: Items in a series are separated by commas, and no comma goes between the compound subject and 'were'. The prepositional phrase in the first item makes it a fair trap.

24.grade_fit_note: Title case with a short verb ('Was') is a little demanding for grade 5 but within range.
24.note: Inside a title, articles are lowercase ('the') and verbs are capitalized however short ('Was'); Chicago, APA and MLA all agree. The title would normally be italicized, but that does not affect the item.

_batch: Key letters are perfectly balanced (6 each of A/B/C/D), and every item is a 2x2 grid, so each site value appears in exactly two options and frequency gives no clue. There is one strong cross-item tell: on every count-axis item, the key is the MIXED cell. It applies one treatment at one site and the opposite at the other, never 'both' or 'neither'. This holds for all 8 Capitalization items (3, 4, 6, 11, 15, 18, 20, 24: the key always has exactly one of the two sites capitalized) and for the count-axis Punctuation items 10, 13, 14, 21 and 23 (comma at one site, none or a semicolon at the other). Item 7 is the only exception: its key uses both comma and question mark. A test-wise student who learns 'pick the option that capitalizes or punctuates one site but not the other' cuts 13 items from 4 choices to 2 without knowing any rule. That raises expected score on those items from 25% to 50%. The grammar items (1, 5, 9, 12, 16, 17, 19, 22) carry no such count axis. In them the all-wrong cell (5B, 9B, 12A, 19A) is often near-dead, which in practice makes them 3-option items. A minor length tell: in item 12 the key is the uniquely shortest option. I saw no recurring wording tell.
